title: Which lines compile?
prompt: Pocket Budget's first playground has a few lines that the Swift compiler will reject. Each option below is a complete snippet on its own. Select **every** snippet that compiles without errors.
hints: Ask two questions of each snippet: is anything assigned twice with `let`, and does any operator mix two values whose types are already fixed?
Bare literals like `1200` and `4.5` have no type until Swift picks one for them, so they can adapt to each other.
An annotation such as `: Double` tells Swift how to read the literal that follows it.
explanation:
Three snippets compile. `var spent` can change, so `+=` is fine. `1200 + 4.5` is two untyped literals, so Swift makes both `Double`. `let fee: Double = 3` reads the integer literal as a `Double` because of the annotation.

The other three fail for the reasons you will meet every week: a `let` can't be reassigned, an `Int` value and a `Double` value can't be added without `Double(rent)`, and a `String` variable can never hold an `Int`.

reassign-let.why: A `let` constant is assigned exactly once. Use `var` if the budget really changes.

increment-var.why: Compiles. `spent` is a variable of type `Int`, and adding an `Int` to it is allowed.

literal-sum.why: Compiles. Both operands are literals, so Swift chooses `Double` for both and `total` is `1204.5`.

mixed-sum.text: `let rent = 1200; let coffee = 4.5; let sum = rent + coffee`
mixed-sum.why: Fails. `rent` is already an `Int` and `coffee` a `Double`; write `Double(rent) + coffee`.

string-to-int.why: Fails. A variable keeps its type for life; `label` can only ever hold a `String`.

annotated-double.why: Compiles. The annotation tells Swift to treat the integer literal `3` as a `Double`.
